subject: seahorse
pitch: A lined seahorse holding on to a strand of seagrass with its curled tail. A ridged body in sunny yellow with thin dark lines and a few white freckles, a little crown of spikes on its head, a long tube snout, a delicate fluttering fin on its back, and big, curious eyes.
reasoning:
I need to design the module around the known SDK functions available, being careful to stick to documented APIs for building the shape and applying surface details like paint, stripes, and decals.

For the seahorse itself, I'm planning to use sweep and chain for the curling body and joints, part and stick for attached elements like eyes, spike for the crown and snout, and ring or along for the ridged texture and stripe patterns around the tube-shaped body and curled tail.

I'm thinking the model should stand about 0.3m tall, with an upright body, forward-angled head, and a tail that curls around a seagrass stem rising from the floor so the lowest point of the whole piece touches y=0.

Working out the spine curve from tail to head, and trying to figure out how to wrap the tail around the grass stem using a helix of points rather than a built-in spiral function, since I'm not sure of the exact path API signatures available.

Still figuring out joints and chains...

Still working out ring orientation...

Since I can't verify the exact API semantics, I'll just commit to something plausible and move forward. I'm planning the seahorse's color palette—sunny yellow body, dark outline markings, white freckles, and translucent fin tones—plus simple grass and ground scenery, then sketching the spine path with the head positioned upright near the top facing forward.

Now I'm working out the joint hierarchy: a neck/trunk chain running from chest down to tail base, a separate head joint aimed toward the snout, a swept tube forming the snout, a sphere-based head shape, and a curling tail chain that wraps around a grass stem positioned off to the side of the body.

Writing coil math for the tail...

I'm wrestling with the joint hierarchy constraint — only one root is allowed, so I'm deciding whether spine and tail should be one continuous chain or separate ones rooted under hips. Simplest path: build a single chain running from the tail tip through the coil up to the head, then sweep the body with a thicker uniform radius while the tail portion gets its own thinner sweep for a better taper.

Now I'm thinking through the seagrass stem as a propless sweep mesh riding the nearest joint, and considering whether to add leaf blades via curved sweeps rather than complicated extrusions. For the dorsal fin, I'm placing it along the back of the body (the -Z side) and defining the membrane between two edge paths.

For the head, I'm fanning out 3-4 crown spikes using base points and direction vectors, then working out how to attach the eyes to the curved head surface by offsetting sphere parts radially from the head center.

Now I'm figuring out the dark ridge detailing along the spine, placing small oriented boxes at intervals along the body's surface normals to create a textured ridge look.

For freckles, I'm scattering tiny white sphere stickers across the surface using a seeded random generator to vary their positions naturally, and setting up a surface lookup from the spine sweep to place things accurately relative to the body's frame at each point along the chain.

I'm now defining the spine as a Catmull chain built from trunk points and sweeping that into the body shape with a constant radius, keeping the head as a separate larger sphere. For the tail, I'm deciding to treat it as its own sweep that starts from the trunk's base and coils separately around the grass, rather than folding the coil into the single spine chain, since mixing the two paths together makes the geometry harder to control.

I'm second-guessing whether to add explicit joints for the head and neck, but since the joint parenting API isn't well-documented, I'm leaning toward skipping extra joints and just letting proximity to the hips root joint and spine chain handle the rigging automatically.

For the fin, I'm sketching two parallel edges along the back of the trunk to form a membrane, with the outer edge offset further out and given slight x-axis variation to simulate fluttering, then planning to move on to the grass stems next.

Now I'm working out the grass blades and leaves, then shifting to the tail coiling around the stem — computing a helix path with decreasing radius and y-values so the tail wraps around the stem base and flares outward at the tip.

Then I'm detailing the surface ridges and dark banding along the spine: sweeping a body along the spine curve, sampling points around its surface at each row position, and placing small boxes at azimuthal intervals to create ridge bumps and thin dark ring-lines between rows.

Next I'm scattering freckles randomly across the body and head surfaces using similar sampling, then positioning crown spikes around the back of the head with upward-leaning directions radiating from a circle at the head's top. Finally I'm sketching the snout as a forward-and-downward sweeping tube extending from the front of the head.

For the eyes, I'm computing symmetric directional offsets from the head center to place white eye spheres with embedded dark pupils and tiny highlights, positioning them on either side of the face. I'm also adding a flattened rock or pebble shape nearby as a base element, partially sunk into the sand.

I'm settling on a color palette for the whole model -- bright yellow body with golden ridges, dark outline accents, cream freckles, white and black eyes, warm snout tone, pale fin color, and green tones for sea grass -- keeping the overall scale around 0.3 meters.

For the fin, I'm planning to use a membrane helper stretched between two edges with a subtle sinusoidal flutter applied to one side. For the ground, I'm using a flattened sphere as a sand disc, and for the ridge and dark outline details I'm placing small boxes along the body to create stylized stitching-like rows.
